title: The Modern Near East
subtitle: 1945–1990 · Decolonisation and the Cold War, the Arab–Israeli Wars, Revolutionary Republics, Oil and the Revolution in Iran

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: Nasser, Sadat, the Assads, Saddam Hussein, the Shah and Khomeini, King Faisal, Ben-Gurion and Arafat

entries.label: Gamal Abdel Nasser
entries.hint: Gamal Abdel Nasser, an army officer who had been a leader of the Free Officers' coup of 23 July 1952, was prime minister from 1954 and president from 1956 until his death on 28 September 1970; he nationalised the Suez Canal, led Egypt into the union with Syria of 1958–1961, became the best-known voice of Arab nationalism and non-alignment, and ruled a single-party state with a large security apparatus; his funeral in Cairo drew crowds of millions.
entries.note: Joel Gordon, Nasser: Hero of the Arab Nation (2006); Anthony Nutting, Nasser (1972); Egypt 1952–today folio.

entries.label: Saddam Hussein
entries.hint: Saddam Hussein, a Ba'thist who took part in the coup of 1968 and as deputy to President al-Bakr controlled the security services, became president on 16 July 1979, when he forced out al-Bakr and had some twenty of the party's leaders tried and shot for a plot; from then until 2003 he ruled Iraq as a personal dictatorship, with a cult of personality, a war against Iran in 1980 and the invasion of Kuwait in 1990.
entries.note: Charles Tripp, A History of Iraq (2000); Joseph Sassoon, Saddam Hussein's Ba'th Party (2012); Iraq 1958–1979 and 1979–2003 folios.

entries.label: Anwar Sadat
entries.hint: Anwar Sadat, Nasser's vice-president, succeeded him in October 1970, purged his rivals in the Corrective Revolution of May 1971, expelled the Soviet advisers in 1972, fought the war of 1973, opened the economy in the infitah, went to Jerusalem in November 1977 and signed the peace treaty with Israel in 1979; he shared the Nobel Peace Prize in 1978 with Menachem Begin and was assassinated by Islamist soldiers on 6 October 1981, during the parade for the anniversary of the crossing.
entries.note: Raymond Baker, Sadat and After (1990); Kirk Beattie, Egypt during the Sadat Years (2000); Nobel Committee (1978).

entries.label: Hafez al-Assad
entries.hint: Hafez al-Assad, an Alawi air force officer and defence minister, took power in the bloodless coup of 13 November 1970 that he called the Corrective Movement, was elected president in 1971 and held the office until his death in June 2000; he built a durable state on the Ba'th party, a loyal officer corps and security services, sent troops into Lebanon in 1976 and became the dominant figure of Syria and a central one in Arab politics.
entries.note: Patrick Seale, Asad of Syria (1988); Raymond Hinnebusch, Syria: Revolution from Above (2001); Syria 1946–today folio.

entries.label: Ruhollah Khomeini
entries.hint: Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, a Shia cleric exiled since 1964 for attacking the shah and the American capitulations, returned to Tehran on 1 February 1979, was made the Supreme Leader under the constitution of December 1979 with its doctrine of the guardianship of the jurist, and led the Islamic Republic through the hostage crisis and the war with Iraq until his death on 3 June 1989.
entries.note: Abrahamian 2008; Baqer Moin, Khomeini: Life of the Ayatollah (1999); Iran 1979–today folio.

entries.label: Mohammad Reza Shah
entries.hint: Mohammad Reza Pahlavi came to the throne in September 1941 on his father's abdication, was restored by the coup of August 1953 that removed Mohammad Mosaddegh, carried through the White Revolution of 1963, celebrated 2,500 years of the monarchy at Persepolis in 1971, established a one-party state in 1975 and left Iran on 16 January 1979 in the face of the revolution; he died in Egypt on 27 July 1980.
entries.note: Ervand Abrahamian, A History of Modern Iran (2008); Abbas Milani, The Shah (2011); Pahlavi 1925–1979 folio.

entries.label: King Faisal of Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: Faisal bin Abdulaziz, crown prince and prime minister, replaced his brother Saud as king in November 1964 after the royal family and the religious establishment had deposed him, introduced television and girls' schooling, led the Arab oil embargo of 1973 and the Islamic solidarity policy against Nasserism and communism, and was shot dead on 25 March 1975 by a nephew.
entries.note: Madawi al-Rasheed, A History of Saudi Arabia (2002); Alexei Vassiliev, The History of Saudi Arabia (1998); Saudi 1902–today folio.

entries.label: Ben-Gurion and the Labour state
entries.hint: David Ben-Gurion, leader of the Yishuv, proclaimed the State of Israel on 14 May 1948 and was prime minister in 1948–1953 and 1955–1963, building a state with a dominant party (Mapai, later Labour), an army, a large immigration and a mixed economy; the Labour bloc governed continuously until the upset election of 17 May 1977, when Menachem Begin's Likud came to power, and from 1984 to 1990 the two blocs shared power in national unity governments.
entries.note: Tom Segev, 1949: The First Israelis (1986); Anita Shapira, Israel: A History (2012); Israel 1948–today folio.

entries.label: Yasser Arafat and the PLO
entries.hint: The Palestine Liberation Organization, set up under Arab League auspices in 1964, was taken over by the guerrilla groups after the defeat of 1967 and from February 1969 chaired by Yasser Arafat of Fatah; the Arab summit in Rabat in 1974 recognised it as the sole legitimate representative of the Palestinian people, and from bases in Jordan, then Lebanon (1970–1982) and Tunis it fought, negotiated and in 1988 declared a state and accepted resolution 242, to the opposition of Israel, which called it a terrorist organisation until 1993.
entries.note: Rashid Khalidi, Palestinian Identity (1997); Yezid Sayigh, Armed Struggle and the Search for State (1997); Palestine 1948–today folio.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The wars of 1948, 1956, 1967 and 1973, the Lebanese and Iran–Iraq wars, the revolutions and the coups

entries.label: The 1948 War and the Nakba
entries.hint: After the UN partition resolution of 29 November 1947 civil war broke out in Palestine and, when the British left and Israel declared independence on 14 May 1948, the armies of Egypt, Transjordan, Syria, Iraq and Lebanon entered; the armistices of 1949 left Israel with more territory than the plan had given it, Jordan the West Bank and Egypt Gaza; some 6,000 Israelis, or one per cent of the Jewish population, died, and some 700,000 to 750,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled, the Nakba (catastrophe) of Palestinian memory and, in Israeli usage, the War of Independence.
entries.note: Benny Morris, The Birth of the Palestinian Refugee Problem Revisited (2004); Avi Shlaim, The Iron Wall (2000); Rashid Khalidi, The Hundred Years' War on Palestine (2020).

entries.label: The Suez Crisis
entries.hint: After Nasser nationalised the Suez Canal Company on 26 July 1956, Britain, France and Israel agreed in secret at Sèvres on a plan: Israel invaded Sinai on 29 October and Britain and France, calling for the belligerents to withdraw, landed at Port Said; American and Soviet pressure and a run on sterling forced them to stop and withdraw, a defeat for the old powers that made Nasser the hero of the Arab world and ended the British premiership of Anthony Eden.
entries.note: Keith Kyle, Suez: Britain's End of Empire in the Middle East (2003); Diane Kunz (ed.), The Economic Diplomacy of the Suez Crisis (1991).

entries.label: The 14 July revolution and the Iraqi coups
entries.hint: The coup of 14 July 1958 by Abd al-Karim Qasim and Abd al-Salam Arif overthrew the monarchy, and the king, the regent and Nuri al-Said were killed; Qasim was himself overthrown and shot in the Ba'thist coup of 8 February 1963, which began a campaign of terror against the communists, the Ba'th was ousted in November 1963 and returned by the coup of July 1968.
entries.note: Hanna Batatu, The Old Social Classes and the Revolutionary Movements of Iraq (1978); Tripp 2000.

entries.label: The Turkish coups
entries.hint: The Turkish army intervened three times: on 27 May 1960, when it removed Adnan Menderes's government, who was hanged in 1961; by the memorandum of 12 March 1971; and by the coup of 12 September 1980 under General Kenan Evren, which suspended parliament and the parties, arrested hundreds of thousands and wrote the constitution of 1982.
entries.note: Erik Zürcher, Turkey: A Modern History (1993); Feroz Ahmad, The Making of Modern Turkey (1993); Turkey 1923–1980 and 1980–today folios.

entries.label: The civil war in North Yemen
entries.hint: The coup of September 1962 against the new imam by officers who proclaimed a republic began a war between the republicans, backed by Nasser's Egypt, which at its height sent some 70,000 men, and the royalists, backed by Saudi Arabia and Jordan; the war of attrition, with gas bombs, tied down Egypt, which withdrew after 1967, and ended with a compromise in 1970.
entries.note: Jesse Ferris, Nasser's Gamble (2013); Asher Orkaby, Beyond the Arab Cold War (2017); Yemen 1900–today folio.

entries.label: The Six-Day War
entries.loc: Sinai, the West Bank and the Golan
entries.hint: After Nasser closed the Straits of Tiran and moved his army into Sinai in May 1967, Israel opened the war on 5 June with an air strike that destroyed the Egyptian air force on the ground and in six days took Sinai and Gaza from Egypt, the West Bank and East Jerusalem from Jordan and the Golan Heights from Syria; some 15,000 to 20,000 Arabs and about 800 Israelis were killed, and the war, seen in Israel as a defensive war of survival and in the Arab world as an aggression, began the occupation of the territories.
entries.note: Michael Oren, Six Days of War (2002); Tom Segev, 1967 (2005); Avi Shlaim 2000.

entries.label: The October War
entries.hint: Egypt and Syria attacked on 6 October 1973, the Day of Atonement and in Ramadan, crossing the Suez Canal and storming the Golan; Israel, which had been caught unprepared, stopped the Syrians and crossed the canal to encircle the Egyptian Third Army, and a ceasefire under resolution 338 came on 22–25 October; the war cost some 2,600 Israeli and 8,000 to 15,000 Arab dead and, for Egypt, restored a sense of honour that allowed it to negotiate, and it brought the Arab oil embargo.
entries.note: Abraham Rabinovich, The Yom Kippur War (2004); Chaim Herzog, The War of Atonement (1975); UN Security Council resolution 338 (22 October 1973).

entries.label: The Lebanese Civil War
entries.hint: A war that began in April 1975 with the shooting of a bus at Ain al-Rummaneh drew in the Maronite militias, the Palestinian and leftist forces, Syria (from 1976), Israel (1978 and 1982), Iran and the multinational force, split Beirut along the Green Line and killed some 120,000 to 150,000 people; the Taif Agreement of 1989 amended the confessional system and Syria's troops stayed until 2005.
entries.note: Fawwaz Traboulsi, A History of Modern Lebanon (2007); Samir Khalaf, Lebanon's Predicament (1987); Lebanon 1943–today folio.

entries.label: The Iranian Revolution
entries.hint: A movement that began in January 1978 with demonstrations in Qom and grew through the cycle of mourning processions, the burning of the Rex Cinema in Abadan in August, the massacre of Black Friday (8 September) and general strikes in the oil fields, united the clergy, the bazaar and the left and overthrew the shah on 11 February 1979 after Khomeini's return; the referendum of 30–31 March approved an Islamic republic by more than 98 per cent.
entries.note: Misagh Parsa, Social Origins of the Iranian Revolution (1989); Nikki Keddie, Modern Iran (2006); Abrahamian 2008.

entries.label: The Iran–Iraq War
entries.hint: Iraq's invasion of Iran on 22 September 1980, after a decade of border disputes and the revolution in Iran, became an eight-year war of attrition, with trench lines, human-wave attacks, missile attacks on cities, the tanker war and Iraq's use of chemical weapons; estimates of the dead run from about 500,000 to a million or more, and the ceasefire of 20 August 1988 left the borders where they had been.
entries.note: Efraim Karsh, The Iran–Iraq War 1980–1988 (2002); Pierre Razoux, The Iran–Iraq War (2015); Iran and Iraq folios.

entries.label: The invasion of Lebanon and Sabra and Shatila
entries.hint: Israel invaded Lebanon on 6 June 1982 to destroy the PLO and reached Beirut, which it besieged until the PLO fighters were evacuated under American guarantees; on 16–18 September, after the assassination of the president-elect Bashir Gemayel, Lebanese Forces militiamen massacred hundreds of Palestinian and Lebanese civilians (estimates 700–3,500) in the camps of Sabra and Shatila, which Israeli forces had surrounded; the Kahan Commission found Israeli officials indirectly responsible.
entries.note: Kahan Commission Report (1983); Rashid Khalidi, Under Siege (1986); Zeev Schiff and Ehud Yaari, Israel's Lebanon War (1984).

entries.label: Hama and the Anfal
entries.hint: In February 1982 the Syrian army, after an uprising by the Muslim Brotherhood, shelled and stormed the city of Hama, killing some 10,000 to 40,000 people by differing estimates; in Iraq the Anfal campaign of 1988 against the Kurds, with chemical weapons at Halabja on 16 March, mass executions and the destruction of villages, killed an estimated 50,000 to 182,000 people, the lower figure being that of many Western analysts and the higher the Kurdish count based on captured Iraqi documents.
entries.note: Raphael Lefèvre, Ashes of Hama (2013); Human Rights Watch, Genocide in Iraq (1993); Joost Hiltermann, A Poisonous Affair (2007).

entries.label: The First Intifada
entries.hint: A rising that began on 9 December 1987 in the Jabalia camp, after four Palestinians were killed in a road accident, spread through the West Bank and Gaza as strikes, stone-throwing, boycotts and committees against the occupation, to which Israel replied with curfews, arrests and live fire; by 1993 some 1,000 or more Palestinians and about 160 Israelis had been killed, and the intifada brought the PLO's 1988 declaration and the Madrid and Oslo talks.
entries.note: B'Tselem statistics (1987–1993); Ze'ev Schiff and Ehud Ya'ari, Intifada (1989); Palestine 1948–today folio.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The Partition Plan, resolutions 242 and 338, Camp David, Taif and the constitutions of the new regimes

entries.label: The UN Partition Plan
entries.hint: General Assembly resolution 181 of 29 November 1947, voted 33 to 13 with 10 abstentions, recommended the partition of Palestine into a Jewish state with some 55 per cent of the land and an Arab state with some 43, with Jerusalem under international administration; the Zionist leadership accepted it and the Arab leaders rejected it, as unjust to the majority population, and civil war followed.
entries.note: UN General Assembly resolution 181 (II); UNSCOP Report (1947); Khalidi 2020.

entries.label: The constitutions of Turkey
entries.hint: The constitution of 1961, written after the first coup and approved by 61 per cent in a referendum, set up a Constitutional Court, a senate and wide civil liberties, and was revised after 1971 to limit them; the constitution of 1982, written under the military regime and approved by 91 per cent in a referendum in which open campaigning against it was forbidden, strengthened the president and the National Security Council and limited the unions and the press.
entries.note: Zürcher 1993; Feroz Ahmad 1993; Turkey 1923–1980 folio.

entries.label: Resolutions 242 and 338
entries.hint: Security Council resolution 242 of 22 November 1967 called for the withdrawal of Israeli armed forces from territories occupied in the recent conflict and for the termination of belligerency and respect for the sovereignty of every state in the area; the English text omits the article before territories and so has been argued over ever since, with the French text saying the territories; resolution 338 of 1973 called for negotiations on its basis.
entries.note: UN Security Council resolutions 242 (1967) and 338 (1973); Avi Shlaim 2000; Khalidi 2020.

entries.label: The Camp David Accords and the peace treaty
entries.hint: After twelve days at Camp David with President Carter, Sadat and Begin signed on 17 September 1978 two frameworks, one for an Egypt–Israel peace and one for the West Bank and Gaza, and on 26 March 1979 the treaty, by which Israel withdrew from Sinai by 1982 in exchange for peace and recognition; Egypt was suspended from the Arab League until 1989 and the Palestinian autonomy plan produced nothing.
entries.note: Camp David Accords (17 September 1978); Egypt–Israel Peace Treaty (26 March 1979); William Quandt, Camp David (1986).

entries.label: The constitution of the Islamic Republic
entries.hint: The constitution approved by referendum on 2–3 December 1979, from a draft revised by the Assembly of Experts to give the Supreme Leader powers over the army, the judiciary and the broadcasting, set up an Islamic republic with an elected president and parliament subject to the veto of the Guardian Council, on the doctrine of the guardianship of the jurist, with the revision of 1989 after Khomeini's death.
entries.note: Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Iran (1979, revised 1989); Said Amir Arjomand, The Turban for the Crown (1988).

entries.label: The Taif Agreement
entries.hint: The Charter of National Reconciliation, agreed by Lebanese deputies at Taif in Saudi Arabia on 22 October 1989 under Saudi, Syrian and American sponsorship, shifted the sectarian balance of the constitution from a ratio of six Christians to five Muslims to equal shares, reduced the powers of the Maronite president, and called for the disbanding of the militias and the withdrawal of Syria's troops to the Beqaa; it ended the civil war in 1990 but its provisions were applied unevenly.
entries.note: Document of National Understanding (Taif, 22 October 1989); Traboulsi 2007; Lebanon 1943–today folio.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: The Brotherhood and Qutb, Khomeini's Islamic government, Zionism and the Jews of the Arab lands, Mecca 1979 and Lebanese Shiism

entries.label: The Jews of the Arab world and Iran
entries.hint: After 1948 some 850,000 Jews left or were forced out of the Arab states and Iran (by common estimates), most for Israel, which received about 600,000 of them, in the Iraqi airlift of 1950–1951, the departures from Egypt after Suez and from Morocco and Algeria; some left under pressure and expulsion, with the confiscation of property, and others were brought by Israeli organisations, and the old communities of the Arab states, some of them more than two thousand years old, all but ended.
entries.note: Yehouda Shenhav, The Arab Jews (2006); Nissim Rejwan, The Jews of Iraq (1985); Abbas Shiblak, The Lure of Zion (1986).

entries.label: The Muslim Brothers and Sayyid Qutb
entries.hint: After an attempt on Nasser's life in October 1954 the Brotherhood was banned and thousands imprisoned, and in prison Sayyid Qutb wrote Milestones (1964), arguing that contemporary society was in a state of pagan ignorance and that believers must form a vanguard; he was hanged on 29 August 1966, and his writing, read by the Islamists of the 1970s and after, became the basis of the radical wing.
entries.note: Richard Mitchell, The Society of the Muslim Brothers (1969); Sayyid Qutb, Ma'alim fi al-tariq (1964); Gilles Kepel, Muslim Extremism in Egypt (1985).

entries.label: Musa al-Sadr and the Shia of Lebanon
entries.hint: Musa al-Sadr, an Iranian-born cleric who came to Tyre in 1959, built the Shia of Lebanon, the poorest of the communities, into a political force with the Supreme Islamic Shia Council (1969) and the Movement of the Deprived and its militia, Amal (1974-75); he disappeared during a visit to Libya in August 1978, and the Libyan government's account that he left for Italy is not accepted by his followers.
entries.note: Fouad Ajami, The Vanished Imam (1986); Traboulsi 2007; Lebanon 1943–today folio.

entries.label: Khomeini's Islamic government
entries.hint: In lectures given at Najaf in January 1970, published as Islamic Government (Hokumat-e Islami), Khomeini argued that kingship was contrary to Islam and that in the absence of the Hidden Imam the jurists should govern in his place; the doctrine, a departure from the Shia clergy's usual quietism, was given in the constitution of 1979 as the basis of the state.
entries.note: Khomeini, Hokumat-e Islami (1970); Moin 1999; Hamid Algar (trans.), Islam and Revolution (1981).

entries.label: The seizure of the Grand Mosque
entries.hint: On 20 November 1979, the first day of the Islamic year 1400, some 200 to 500 armed men under Juhayman al-Utaybi seized the Grand Mosque of Mecca, proclaiming one of their number the Mahdi and denouncing the Saudi dynasty; after a fortnight of fighting in which the government used French advisers and a fatwa from the scholars the mosque was retaken on 4 December, and the officially announced toll was 127 troops and 117 militants killed, with Juhayman and 63 others publicly executed in January 1980.
entries.note: Yaroslav Trofimov, The Siege of Mecca (2007); Thomas Hegghammer and Stéphane Lacroix, The Meccan Rebellion (2011); Saudi 1902–today folio.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: Umm Kulthum and Fairuz, Mahfouz, the Iranian New Wave and Darwish

entries.label: Naguib Mahfouz and the Nobel Prize
entries.hint: Naguib Mahfouz's Cairo Trilogy (Bayn al-Qasrayn, Qasr al-Shawq, al-Sukkariyya, 1956–1957), which follows a Cairo merchant family from 1917 to 1944, and later Children of Gebelawi (serialised 1959, banned in Egypt and published in Lebanon) made the novel the main genre of Arabic literature; in 1988 he became the first Arabic writer to win the Nobel Prize in Literature.
entries.note: Naguib Mahfouz, al-Thulathiyya (1956–57); Nobel Committee (1988); Rasheed El-Enany, Naguib Mahfouz (1993).
keywords: Naguib Mahfouz Cairo Trilogy Bayn al-Qasrayn

entries.label: Mahmoud Darwish and the poetry of exile
entries.hint: Mahmoud Darwish, born in al-Birwa in the Galilee in 1941, whose family fled to Lebanon in 1948 and returned to Israel as so-called present absentees, published Identity Card (Bitaqat huwiyya) in 1964 and became the poet of the Palestinian cause, living in Beirut and Paris and writing the draft of the declaration of independence of the Palestinian National Council in 1988; with Nizar Qabbani in Syria and Badr Shakir al-Sayyab in Iraq he belonged to a generation of poets of the free verse.
entries.note: Mahmoud Darwish, Sajjil ana arabi; Khaled Mattawa, Mahmoud Darwish (2014); Palestine 1948–today folio.

entries.label: Umm Kulthum and Fairuz
entries.hint: Umm Kulthum, who after the defeat of 1967 gave concerts, including one in Paris, to raise funds for the war effort, and whose funeral procession through Cairo on 3 February 1975 was followed by crowds of millions; Fairuz, with the Rahbani brothers, made at the Baalbek festival and on Lebanese radio a Lebanese song of folklore and nostalgia which became in the civil war the voice of the country; the two women's recordings remain the common culture of the region.
entries.note: Virginia Danielson, The Voice of Egypt (1997); Rogan, The Arabs (2009).

entries.label: The Iranian New Wave
entries.hint: Dariush Mehrjui's The Cow (1969), based on a story by Gholam-Hossein Sa'edi, and Bahram Beyzai, Sohrab Shahid-Saless and Abbas Kiarostami (whose first films were made for the Institute for the Intellectual Development of Children and Young Adults) made a cinema of the poor and of poetic realism, on the model of the poems of Forugh Farrokhzad; much of its reputation grew abroad after the revolution.
entries.note: Hamid Naficy, A Social History of Iranian Cinema, vol. 2 (2011); Pahlavi 1925–1979 folio.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Ba'thism and pan-Arabism, Shariati and Al-e Ahmad, Said's Orientalism and religious Zionism

entries.label: Ba'thism and pan-Arabism
entries.hint: The Ba'th (Resurrection) party, founded at Damascus in April 1947 by the Syrians Michel Aflaq, a Christian, and Salah al-Din al-Bitar, preached that the Arabs were one nation and one mission, with unity, freedom and socialism; after Suez, pan-Arabism, with Nasser as its figure, produced the United Arab Republic of Egypt and Syria (February 1958–September 1961), which dissolved in a Syrian coup and left the movement divided among its rival states.
entries.note: Michel Aflaq, Fi sabil al-ba'th (1959); Albert Hourani, Arabic Thought in the Liberal Age (1962); Malcolm Kerr, The Arab Cold War (1971).

entries.label: Al-e Ahmad and Shariati
entries.hint: Jalal Al-e Ahmad's essay Gharbzadegi (1962), called Westoxication or Occidentosis, which attacked the uncritical adoption of Western goods and ideas, and the lectures of Ali Shariati at the Husseiniyeh Ershad (1969–1972), which presented Shiism as a revolutionary ideology of the oppressed against tyranny, shaped a generation of Iranian students who joined the revolution of 1979.
entries.note: Jalal Al-e Ahmad, Gharbzadegi (1962); Ali Shariati, Collected Works; Ervand Abrahamian, Radical Islam (1989).

entries.label: Gush Emunim and religious Zionism
entries.hint: After the conquests of 1967 the students of Rabbi Zvi Yehuda Kook, who held that the state was the beginning of redemption, formed the Gush Emunim (Bloc of the Faithful) in 1974 and founded the settlements of Kiryat Arba (1968–71) and Ofra, Sebastia and others, claiming the biblical land of Judea and Samaria; their movement was supported by the Likud and opposed by the Peace Now movement of 1978 and the Palestinians, who saw in the settlements a loss of land.
entries.note: Ehud Sprinzak, The Ascendance of Israel's Radical Right (1991); Gershom Gorenberg, The Accidental Empire (2006); Israel 1948–today folio.
keywords: Gush Emunim Bloc of the Faithful

entries.label: Edward Said and Orientalism
entries.hint: Edward Said, a Palestinian-born professor at Columbia, argued in Orientalism (1978) that Western scholarship, art and literature about the East had been an institution of power which made the Orient a place of otherness, with consequences for colonial policy; the book, praised and attacked, led the field of postcolonial studies and a long argument about Said's treatment of the scholars.
entries.note: Edward Said, Orientalism (1978); Bernard Lewis, The Question of Orientalism (1982); Robert Irwin, For Lust of Knowing (2006).

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: OPEC and the oil shocks, land reform, infitah and the Gulf boom

entries.label: The nationalisation of Iranian oil
entries.hint: The Majlis voted on 15 March 1951 to nationalise the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company, and Prime Minister Mosaddegh's government took over Abadan; Britain withdrew its staff, boycotted the oil and with the United States prepared the coup of 19 August 1953, after which the consortium of 1954 gave British Petroleum 40 per cent, a group of American companies 40, Shell 14 and the French 6, with the National Iranian Oil Company owning the installations on paper and sharing the profits equally.
entries.note: Ervand Abrahamian, The Coup (2013); Yergin 1991; Mostafa Elm, Oil, Power and Principle (1992).

entries.label: Land reform and nationalisation
entries.hint: Egypt's Agrarian Reform Law of September 1952 limited holdings to 200 feddans and the socialist decrees of July 1961 nationalised banks and large firms, Iraq's land law of 1958 limited holdings and Iran's White Revolution of January 1963 distributed land from the crown, the church and big landlords to some 1.5 million families; the reforms broke the old landowning class but created state-dependent peasants and mixed economic results.
entries.note: Roger Owen and Şevket Pamuk, A History of Middle East Economies in the Twentieth Century (1998); Ann Lambton, The Persian Land Reform (1969).
keywords: Egypt Agrarian Reform Law of September

entries.label: OPEC, the embargo and the oil shocks
entries.hint: The Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries, founded in Baghdad in September 1960 by Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and Venezuela, and in October 1973 the Arab members of OAPEC, who cut production and embargoed the United States and the Netherlands after the October War, brought a fourfold rise in the price within months and a second rise after the Iranian revolution in 1979; the oil revenue of the OPEC members rose from some 20 billion dollars a year in 1972 to well over 200 billion in 1980.
entries.note: Daniel Yergin, The Prize (1991); OPEC statutes (1960); Rasheed 2002.
keywords: Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries

entries.label: Infitah and the bread riots
entries.hint: Sadat's open-door policy, announced in his October Paper of April 1974, invited foreign and private investment, ended the Soviet-style planning and gave rise to a new class of importers and contractors; the cut of subsidies on bread and basic goods announced on 17 January 1977 brought the bread riots of 18–19 January, in which some 80 were killed, and a reversal of the cuts.
entries.note: Beattie 2000; Owen and Pamuk 1998; Egypt 1952–today folio.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: The Aswan High Dam, the nuclear programmes and radio, the cassette and the transistor

entries.label: The transistor, the cassette and the radio
entries.hint: Cairo's Voice of the Arabs, a radio station set up in 1953 and heard on cheap transistor sets across the region, carried Nasser's speeches to Arab publics over the heads of their governments, and in the revolution of 1978–1979 the tapes of Khomeini's sermons, sent from exile in Najaf and Paris and copied on cassette in the bazaars, passed outside the censorship; the new media made politics a mass affair.
entries.note: James Gelvin, The Modern Middle East (2005); Annabelle Sreberny and Ali Mohammadi, Small Media, Big Revolution (1994); Rogan 2009.

entries.label: The nuclear programmes and Osirak
entries.hint: Israel built a reactor at Dimona with French help from 1958, and is widely thought to have developed nuclear weapons by the late 1960s, which it neither confirms nor denies; Iraq bought a reactor, Osirak, from France in 1976, which Israeli aircraft destroyed on 7 June 1981, and the shah's Iran began its nuclear plan, with the Bushehr plant contracted to the German Siemens in 1975 and left unfinished after the revolution.
entries.note: Avner Cohen, Israel and the Bomb (1998); International Atomic Energy Agency reports.

entries.label: The Aswan High Dam
entries.hint: The High Dam on the Nile, begun in January 1960 with Soviet finance and engineers after the Western withdrawal of its offer in 1956, completed in 1970 and inaugurated in January 1971, created Lake Nasser, which holds 130 or more cubic kilometres of water, and gave Egypt control of the flood, electric power and extra crops, at the price of the loss of silt, salt and the displacement of some 50,000 to 100,000 Nubians from their land.
entries.note: Tom Little, High Dam at Aswan (1965); Egypt 1952–today folio.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: The Cold War alliances, Khartoum and Rabat, Sadat's Jerusalem and the refugee regime

entries.label: UNRWA and the refugee question
entries.hint: General Assembly resolution 194 of December 1948 said that refugees wishing to return to their homes and live at peace should be permitted to do so and that compensation should be paid to those who chose not to; the UN Relief and Works Agency was set up in December 1949 and began operations in May 1950 for about 900,000 registered refugees, and the question of return, which Palestinians hold to be a right and Israel has rejected as a threat to its Jewish majority, has remained at the centre of the dispute.
entries.note: UN General Assembly resolution 194 (III), 11 December 1948; resolution 302 (IV); Benny Morris 2004; Khalidi 2020.

entries.label: The Cold War alliances
entries.hint: The Baghdad Pact of 1955 among Turkey, Iraq, Britain, Pakistan and Iran, backed by the United States, was answered by Nasser's arms deal with Czechoslovakia of September 1955 and the Soviet alliance, and the Eisenhower Doctrine of January 1957 offered American aid against communism; the Soviet position in Egypt ended with the expulsion of its advisers by Sadat in July 1972 and the move to the American side.
entries.note: Malcolm Kerr, The Arab Cold War (1971); Salim Yaqub, Containing Arab Nationalism (2004); Rogan 2009.

entries.label: Khartoum, the three noes and Rabat
entries.hint: The Arab summit at Khartoum in September 1967 agreed what has been called the three noes (no peace, no recognition, no negotiation with Israel) and financial aid to Egypt and Jordan from the oil states, while the Rabat summit of October 1974 recognised the PLO as the sole legitimate representative of the Palestinian people, which took the claim to the West Bank from Jordan's King Hussein.
entries.note: Khartoum Resolutions (1 September 1967); Rabat Summit Resolutions (1974); Shlaim 2000.

entries.label: Sadat in Jerusalem
entries.hint: Sadat flew to Jerusalem on 19 November 1977 and addressed the Knesset the next day, the first Arab leader to visit Israel, offering peace in exchange for the withdrawal from the territories and the rights of the Palestinians, a step praised in the West and Israel and denounced by the PLO, Syria and most Arab states, which broke relations with Egypt after 1979.
entries.note: Anwar Sadat, In Search of Identity (1977); Quandt 1986; Kenneth Stein, Heroic Diplomacy (1999).

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: The population surge, the earthquakes and the displaced of the Lebanese war

entries.label: The population surge and the new megacities
entries.hint: With falling mortality and high fertility the population of Egypt grew from some 19 million in 1947 to over 50 million by 1990, that of Iran from about 15 to over 55 million, and the cities, Cairo from about two million in 1947 to some nine million by 1990 (as a metropolitan area) and Tehran from one to over six million, took in the migration from the villages and the schools filled with the young.
entries.note: Owen and Pamuk 1998; Janet Abu-Lughod, Cairo: 1001 Years of the City Victorious (1971); national censuses.

entries.label: The displaced of the Lebanese war
entries.hint: The sectarian lines of the war moved hundreds of thousands of Lebanese from mixed areas into homogeneous ones, for example the Christian mountain and east Beirut or the Shia southern suburbs, and hundreds of thousands more left the country for the Gulf, Europe, Australia and the Americas, which added to a diaspora already larger than the resident population.
entries.note: Traboulsi 2007; Samir Khalaf, Civil and Uncivil Violence in Lebanon (2002); Lebanon 1943–today folio.

entries.label: The Tabas and Manjil earthquakes
entries.hint: The earthquake of 16 September 1978 destroyed the town of Tabas in eastern Iran and killed between 15,000 and 25,000 of its people, and that of 21 June 1990 at Manjil and Rudbar in the north, with a magnitude of 7.4, killed an estimated 35,000 to 50,000 and left half a million without a home, showing the weakness of rural building.
entries.note: Nicholas Ambraseys and Charles Melville, A History of Persian Earthquakes (1982); USGS earthquake catalogue.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: Women, the ma'abarot and the camps, the Kurds and the migrant workers of the Gulf

entries.label: The Kurds in four states
entries.hint: The Kurds, some 20 to 30 million people divided among Turkey, Iraq, Iran and Syria, saw the short-lived Republic of Mahabad in Iran (January–December 1946), the revolt of Mustafa Barzani in Iraq (1961–1975), the denial of the Kurdish language in Turkey after 1980 and the Anfal campaign of 1988; the borders and the politics of four states, which Kurds saw as the cause of their division, kept the movements separate.
entries.note: David McDowall, A Modern History of the Kurds (1996); Martin van Bruinessen, Agha, Shaikh and State (1992); Kurdish folios.

entries.label: The camps and the stateless
entries.hint: The camps set up by UNRWA in Gaza, the West Bank, Jordan, Lebanon and Syria, where tents became concrete rooms over the years, held perhaps a third of the registered refugees, with the services of the agency, a political life under the PLO factions and, in Lebanon, a legal bar on many professions and on property; the refugees' status varied from citizenship in Jordan to statelessness in Lebanon.
entries.note: Rosemary Sayigh, Palestinians: From Peasants to Revolutionaries (1979); Julie Peteet, Landscape of Hope and Despair (2005).

entries.label: The ma'abarot and the Mizrahim
entries.hint: The mass immigration of 1948–1951, which doubled the Jewish population of Israel, with 330,000 or more Jews from Asia and North Africa, was housed first in tent and tin-hut transit camps, the ma'abarot, with hardship, disease and little work; the Mizrahim's experience of discrimination in housing, education and the party machine was the source of the Wadi Salib riots of 1959 and the Black Panthers of 1971 and of the Likud vote of 1977.
entries.note: Tom Segev 1986; Sami Smooha, Israel: Pluralism and Conflict (1978); Shenhav 2006.

entries.label: Women, the Family Protection Law and the hijab
entries.hint: The Family Protection Law of 1967 and 1975 in Iran limited polygamy and men's right of divorce and gave women the right to seek a divorce in court, and women voted and sat in parliament from 1963; after the revolution the law was set aside, the veil, which many women had worn in the demonstrations of 1978 as a sign of opposition, became compulsory in public in 1983, and women stayed in the universities and the professions in growing numbers.
entries.note: Haleh Afshar, Islam and Feminisms (1998); Nikki Keddie, Women in the Middle East (2007); Abrahamian 2008.

entries.label: The migrant workers of the Gulf boom
entries.hint: The oil boom drew in millions of foreign workers, first Palestinians, Egyptians, Yemenis and Lebanese and by the 1980s increasingly South and Southeast Asians, who made up a majority of the labour force in Kuwait, Qatar and the Emirates under the sponsorship (kafala) system, with remittances that became a main income of Egypt, Yemen, Pakistan and India; the Gulf war of 1990 sent hundreds of thousands home.
entries.note: Owen and Pamuk 1998; Andrzej Kapiszewski, Nationals and Expatriates (2001); Kuwait 1961–today folio.
